Question: Circle \(C_1\) has its center \(O\) lying on circle \(C_2.\) The two circles meet at \(X\) and \(Y.\) Point \(Z\) in the exterior of \(C_1\) lies on circle \(C_2\) and \(XZ = 13,\) \(OZ = 11,\) and \(YZ = 7.\) What is the radius of circle \(C_1?\)
Solution:
Let \(r\) be the radius of \(C_1\), so \(OX=OY=r\). These segments are also equal chords of \(C_2\), allowing us to relate the angles at \(Z\).

The intersection points \(X,Y\) divide \(C_2\) into an arc inside \(C_1\) and an arc outside it. The inside arc contains \(O\), while the outside arc contains \(Z\). Equal chords \(OX\) and \(OY\) make \(O\) the midpoint of the inside arc. The inscribed-angle theorem therefore gives
\[
\angle XZO=\angle OZY.
\]
Choose \(P\) on segment \(ZX\) with \(ZP=7\), which is possible because \(ZX=13\). Triangles \(ZPO\) and \(ZYO\) have \(ZP=ZY=7\), their common side \(ZO\), and equal included angles at \(Z\). They are congruent by SAS, so
\[
OP=OY=OX=r.
\]
Thus triangle \(OPX\) is isosceles. Let \(H\) be the foot of the perpendicular from \(O\) to \(PX\). This perpendicular bisects \(PX\). Since \(PX=13-7=6\), we have
\[
HX=HP=3,\qquad ZH=7+3=10.
\]
Apply the Pythagorean theorem first to \(OZH\), then to \(OXH\):
\[
OH^2=11^2-10^2=21,
\qquad r^2=OH^2+3^2=30.
\]
A radius is positive, so \(r=\boxed{\sqrt{30}}\), choice E.
